## Motivation {#motivation}

A sequence model can carry information forward in a state instead of revisiting every earlier input at each step.
A state-space model specifies how that state evolves with inputs and how outputs are read from it.
A state summarises the past information that a model uses to update its future predictions.
The state need not be the smallest possible representation or a directly measurable physical quantity.
This note follows the construction from continuous dynamics to a discrete sequence layer, then explains how the state can represent history.

## Continuous linear dynamics {#continuous-system}

Let $h(t)\in\mathbb R^N$ be the state, $u(t)\in\mathbb R^m$ the input, and $y(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ the output.
A continuous linear state-space system is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \dot h(t)&=Ah(t)+Bu(t),\\
  y(t)&=Ch(t)+Du(t).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The matrices have compatible shapes: $A$ is $N\times N$, $B$ is $N\times m$, $C$ is $p\times N$, and $D$ is $p\times m$.
The feedthrough term $Du$ bypasses the state and can act like a learned skip connection.
If these matrices are constant, the dynamics are linear and time-invariant.
The zero-initial-state input–output map obeys superposition and commutes with time shifts; a fixed nonzero initial state adds a [homogeneous response]{.term key="homogeneous-response"}.
See [Mamba, Section 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752) for this construction as a sequence layer.

## Discretisation and the meaning of a step {#discretisation}

Discretisation turns continuous parameters into a recurrence for sampled inputs.
Assume $A$ and $B$ are constant over the integration interval.
Let $\Delta>0$ be a step size, and assume the input is held constant during each step.
Zero-order hold gives

$$
  \bar A=e^{\Delta A},\qquad
  \bar B=\left(\int_0^\Delta e^{sA}\,ds\right)B.
$$

Here $e^{\Delta A}$ is the [matrix exponential]{.term key="matrix-exponential"}, rather than applying a scalar exponential separately to each entry.
The integral formula remains valid when $A$ is singular.
For invertible $A$, it becomes $\bar B=A^{-1}(e^{\Delta A}-I)B$.
In a sequence model, $\Delta$ can be a learned parameter; it is not automatically a physical sensor's sampling interval.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: zero-order hold"}

The variation-of-constants solution over one interval is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  h(t+\Delta)
  &=e^{\Delta A}h(t)\\
  &\quad+\int_t^{t+\Delta}e^{(t+\Delta-s)A}Bu(s)\,ds.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Set $u(s)=u_k$ on that interval and change variables to $r=t+\Delta-s$.
The input contribution is then $(\int_0^\Delta e^{rA}\,dr)Bu_k$.
If $A$ is invertible, integrate $\frac{d}{dr}e^{rA}=Ae^{rA}$ to obtain the alternative expression above.
For $A=0$, the integral gives $\bar B=\Delta B$ directly.

:::

Other numerical methods approximate the same differential equation differently.
For a scalar homogeneous mode $\dot h=\lambda h$, write $z=\Delta\lambda$.

| Method | One-step multiplier | Accuracy and stability |
|---|---|---|
| Exact / ZOH homogeneous part | $e^z$ | Exact for the constant linear dynamics. |
| Forward Euler | $1+z$ | First order; stability requires $\lvert1+z\rvert<1$. |
| Backward Euler | $(1-z)^{-1}$ | First order; maps the open left half-plane inside the unit disk. |
| Trapezoidal / bilinear | $(1+z/2)/(1-z/2)$ | Second order; also preserves that scalar stability region. |
| Classical RK4 | $1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24$ | Fourth order; has a bounded explicit stability region. |

For driven systems, endpoint input conventions must also agree.
Trapezoidal integration averages the two endpoint forcing terms; the common S4 bilinear parameterisation is a discrete sequence-layer convention and should not be mixed silently with a different indexing of the input.

## A recurrence and a convolution can represent the same layer {#convolution}

Use the sequence convention

$$
  h_k=\bar A h_{k-1}+\bar B u_k,\qquad
  y_k=Ch_k+Du_k,
$$

with $h_{-1}=0$.
For constant matrices, the output is a causal convolution plus feedthrough:

$$
  y_k=\sum_{j=0}^k K_j u_{k-j}+Du_k,
  \qquad K_j=C\bar A^j\bar B.
$$

This allows one layer to be evaluated on a whole sequence using convolution or incrementally using its state.
An alternative convention $h_{k+1}=\bar Ah_k+\bar Bu_k$, $y_k=Ch_k$ introduces a one-step delay in the state-mediated output.
Write the convention before comparing kernels or transfer functions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: unrolling the recurrence"}

With the chosen initial condition,

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  h_0&=\bar Bu_0,\\
  h_1&=\bar A\bar Bu_0+\bar Bu_1,\\
  h_k&=\sum_{j=0}^k\bar A^j\bar B u_{k-j}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Multiplication by $C$ gives the kernel coefficients.
For the associated infinite sequence, its formal transfer function is

$$
  K(z)=C(I-\bar A z^{-1})^{-1}\bar B+D,
$$

where the geometric series converges in its region of convergence.
Convolution becomes multiplication after a compatible Fourier or $z$ transform.
The relation uses time-invariance; input-dependent state transitions generally require another computation.

:::

## Example: a scalar memory {#scalar-memory}

Take $h_k=\tfrac12h_{k-1}+u_k$, $y_k=h_k$, and $h_{-1}=0$.
For an input equal to $1$ at $k=0$ and $0$ afterward, the outputs are $1,\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\ldots$.
The state retains a decaying contribution from the earlier input, and the same sequence gives the layer's convolution kernel.
This example exposes the memory timescale directly: changing the multiplier changes how rapidly a past contribution shrinks.
It also shows why a state value need not be a physical measurement; here it is an accumulated summary chosen by the recurrence.

## Polynomial projection and HiPPO {#hippo}

HiPPO defines a memory state through the projection of an input history onto polynomial basis functions under a specified time-dependent measure.
It is a finite-dimensional approximation, not exact storage of an arbitrary full history.
Here, consider one scalar input channel $u(t)\in\mathbb R$; the construction can be applied separately to multiple channels.
For the scaled Legendre construction at $t>0$, use the uniform probability measure $ds/t$ over $[0,t]$.
Let $P_n$ be the usual Legendre polynomial on $[-1,1]$, and define an orthonormal basis on $[0,1]$:

$$
  p_n(r)=\sqrt{2n+1}\,P_n(2r-1).
$$

The shift $2r-1$ and normalisation matter.
The first $N$ memory coefficients are

$$
  c_n(t)=\frac1t\int_0^t u(s)p_n(s/t)\,ds.
$$

Here $n=0,\ldots,N-1$ indexes the retained basis functions.
They specify the best squared-error approximation in the span of those basis functions under the chosen measure.
The corresponding dynamics have the form

$$
  \dot c(t)=\frac1t\bigl(Ac(t)+Bu(t)\bigr).
$$

In this sign convention, $B_n=\sqrt{2n+1}$ and

$$
  A_{nm}=
  \begin{cases}
  -\sqrt{(2n+1)(2m+1)},&n>m,\\
  -(n+1),&n=m,\\
  0,&n<m.
  \end{cases}
$$

This is a linear time-varying system in physical time.
Neural networks do not require time-invariant dynamics.
The formula and memory interpretation follow [HiPPO, Section 3 and Appendix D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.07669).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the moving basis and the factor 1/t"}

Differentiate the upper limit, the factor $1/t$, and the basis argument:

$$
  R_n(r)=p_n(r)+rp_n'(r),
$$

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \dot c_n(t)
  &=\frac{u(t)p_n(1)}{t}\\
  &\quad-\frac1{t^2}\int_0^t u(s)R_n(s/t)\,ds.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Here $R_n$ groups the terms from differentiating the normaliser and the moving basis.
This polynomial has degree $n$.
Expand it in the orthonormal basis through degree $n$; its coefficients are

$$
  -A_{nm}=\int_0^1
  \bigl[p_n(r)+rp_n'(r)\bigr]p_m(r)\,dr.
$$

Coefficients for $m>n$ vanish by orthogonality, giving the lower-triangular structure.
For $n=0$, $c_0(t)$ is the running average, so $\dot c_0=(u-c_0)/t$.
This checks the signs and scaling.
With logarithmic time $\tau=\ln t$, define $\tilde c(\tau)=c(e^\tau)$.
Then

$$
  \frac{d\tilde c}{d\tau}=A\tilde c+B u(e^\tau).
$$

Both terms in the original dynamics had the factor $1/t$, so no extra factor $t$ remains on the input.

:::

## What S4 adds {#s4}

S4 uses structured state-space parameters to make long convolution kernels efficient to compute.
Its construction relates a HiPPO-derived matrix to a normal matrix plus a low-rank correction, then changes basis to obtain diagonal-plus-low-rank structure.
Fast kernel evaluation uses that structure and efficient resolvent calculations, rather than repeatedly forming dense matrix powers.
See [S4, Sections 3–4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00396).

Training can evaluate the fixed sequence kernel in parallel, and generation can update a fixed-size recurrent state.
The [Woodbury identity](../mathematics/matrix-dynamics.qmd#woodbury) explains why a low-rank correction is computationally useful.
A generic diagonal-plus-low-rank matrix is not automatically stable; the parameterisation and constraints matter.

## From fixed memory to selective memory {#selectivity}

An LTI kernel depends on a time lag, not on the content of the current token.
Mamba makes selected state-space parameters depend on the input, allowing memory retention, input injection, and readout to change with content.
This removes the single fixed convolution kernel while retaining an efficient scan over affine state updates.
The [Mamba review](../../literature-review/theory/mamba.qmd) gives the actual parameter roles and the scan derivation.

At fixed model width and state size, recurrent SSM inference stores a state whose size does not grow with the processed sequence length.
For standard attention with a KV cache, each new token reads a growing set of stored keys and values.
Whole-sequence attention cost and cost per generated token are different quantities; hardware, model dimensions, and implementation must be specified for a numerical speed comparison.

## Connections and boundaries {#connections}

The recurrence–convolution equivalence above assumes fixed coefficients and the stated initial condition.
State-space notation alone does not establish linearity, time-invariance, stability, or an exact representation of the full history.
Those properties depend on the update rule, parameter constraints, and the information retained in the state.

[Matrix structure and dynamics](../mathematics/matrix-dynamics.qmd) explains normality, long-time stability, transient amplification, and low-rank inverse corrections.
[Loss](loss.qmd#loss-and-risk) explains the squared-error objective used in polynomial approximation.
[KV caching](kv-cache.qmd) develops the attention-memory comparison.
The [Mamba review](../../literature-review/theory/mamba.qmd) gives the input-dependent parameter roles and scan derivation.
The recurrence and kernel formulations follow [S4, Section 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00396); the discretisation notation follows [Mamba, Section 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752).
